Live Analysis walkthrough
xrefcode.com / docs / cli / live-alloc

$ xref live alloc

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com
On this page
  1. Usage
  2. Arguments and options
  3. Examples
  4. Reading the output
  5. Limits

Count a running process's allocations by call site: uprobes on the allocator's malloc, calloc, realloc and free report, for every call stack and every function, how many allocations it made, how many bytes, and how many bytes are still allocated at the end. The stacks are unwound from .eh_frame while the capture runs, so a long capture of a busy allocator stays small. Recordings weighted by bytes are read by profile report and compared by profile diff.

live heap needs no uprobes and keeps the process at full speed, but it sees only memory the allocator maps from the kernel. live alloc sees every call, so it answers questions like "does this allocate per row?" or "does the idle daemon allocate at all?".

Usage

xref live alloc [OPTIONS] --pid <PID>

Arguments and options

Options

--pid <PID>
Target process ID.
--duration <DURATION>
How long to observe, e.g. 10s or 500ms; also ends at process exit or Ctrl-C.
default 10s
--stack-bytes <STACK_BYTES>
User stack bytes copied at each allocation for DWARF unwinding.
default 4096
--allocator <ALLOCATOR>
The allocator to trace: a path the process maps that exports malloc and free (by default the executable, then other libraries, then libc; the others are listed).
--out <OUT>
Directory (new) for alloc.xprof (bytes allocated by stack) and live.xprof (bytes still allocated at the end), for xref profile report and xref profile diff.
--top <TOP>
Rows in each table of the report.
default 20
--json
Print the capture and the report as JSON.

Examples

Command
# Who allocates, and what stays allocated, over ten seconds:
sudo xref -b daemon live alloc --pid 1234 --duration 10s
# Before and after a change: compare bytes allocated by function.
sudo xref -b daemon live alloc --pid 1234 --duration 10s --out before
sudo xref -b daemon live alloc --pid 1234 --duration 10s --out after
xref -b daemon profile diff before/alloc.xprof after/alloc.xprof

A program that, every millisecond, allocates and frees ten 64-byte rows, keeps one 16-byte block and grows a buffer with realloc:

live alloc: 2069 ms, allocator /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 (1 threads, 0 unattached, 0 lost and 0 undecoded records, stop duration)
allocations: 21467 (10375.5/s), 211.1 MiB; frees: 17890 (0 of blocks from before), reallocs: 1788
live at the end: 29.0 KiB in 1790 blocks allocated while observed
functions by allocations (callees included):
     allocs       bytes        live  function
      17890     1.1 MiB         0 B  target:alloc_row
       1789    28.0 KiB    28.0 KiB  target:keep_style
       1788   210.0 MiB     1.0 KiB  target:grow_buffer

Reading the output

  • allocs and bytes count the blocks allocated while xref observed, by malloc, calloc and realloc. A realloc that moves a block counts as one allocation of the new size. live is what those blocks still hold at the end.
  • Only the outermost allocator call of a thread counts, so glibc's realloc, which calls malloc and free inside, is not counted twice.
  • frees counts free calls; those of blocks allocated before xref attached (of blocks from before) are part of it, with an unknown size. A block moved by realloc is not a free.
  • The function table lists functions of the program and of its libraries, the allocator's own file left out, by the allocations under them.
  • profile report prints alloc.xprof as bytes allocated and live.xprof as bytes still allocated; profile diff compares two recordings of the same kind.
  • The allocator is the first mapped file that exports malloc and free, searched in this order: the executable, other libraries (an interposed jemalloc or mimalloc), then the C library. Other files exporting them are listed as a warning; --allocator PATH picks one when the process calls another (for example a plugin loaded with its own allocator).

Limits

  • Needs root (uprobes). Every allocator call stops the thread twice (entry and return) and copies --stack-bytes of stack, so a program that allocates millions of times a second slows down while it is observed.
  • An allocator without exported symbols, such as Rust's jemallocator linked statically, cannot be traced; Rust's default system allocator can.
  • Libraries loaded during the capture are not unwound.
  • Threads are found by scanning /proc every 25 ms: a thread that starts and ends between two scans is not observed.
